text: A gyro monorail, also known as a gyroscopic or gyro-stabilized monorail, is a single-rail land vehicle that uses the gyroscopic action of spinning wheels to maintain balance on a single rail, overcoming its inherent instability. This technology was developed by Louis Brennan, August Scherl, and Pyotr Shilovsky, each building full-scale working prototypes in the early 20th century. A later version was developed in the US in 1962 by Ernest F. Swinney, Harry Ferreira, and Louis E. Swinney. Despite its advantages, the gyro monorail was never developed beyond the prototype stage. One key benefit cited by Shilovsky is the suppression of hunting oscillation, a speed limitation in conventional railways, and the ability to make sharper turns than modern high-speed trains like the TGV, as the vehicle automatically banks on curves like an aircraft, eliminating lateral centrifugal acceleration. A major drawback is that most vehicles—passenger or freight—would require powered gyroscopes to remain upright. Unlike lateral shifting or reaction wheels, the gyroscopic system is statically stable, meaning the control system functions primarily as a roll damper. Louis Brennan developed a 22-tonne (22-long-ton; 24-short-ton) unladen prototype and filed his first monorail patent in 1903. His first demonstration model was a 30.0-by-11.8-inch (762 by 300 mm) box containing the balancing system, which prompted the Army Council to recommend £10,000 for development, though this was vetoed by the Financial Department. The Army later provided £2,000 from various sources. Within this budget, Brennan built a larger model, 6.0 by 1.5 feet (1.83 by 0.46 m), balanced by two 5.0-inch (127 mm) diameter gyroscope rotors, which is still on display at the London Science Museum. The track was laid in the grounds of Brennan’s house in Gillingham, Kent, using ordinary gas piping on wooden sleepers with a 50-foot (15 m) wire rope bridge, sharp corners, and slopes up to one in five. Brennan demonstrated this model in a 1907 lecture to the Royal Society, showing it running back and forth "on a taught and slender wire" under his control. The reduced-scale railway validated the War Department’s initial interest, though funding ceased after the 1906 Liberal government election. In 1907, the India Office approved £6,000 (equivalent to £801,733 in 2023) for development in the North West Frontier, and in 1908, the Durbar of Kashmir provided £5,000 (equivalent to £659,406 in 2023), with nearly all funds spent by January 1909, followed by an additional £2,000 (equivalent to £263,333 in 2023). On 15 October 1909, the railcar ran under its own power for the first time, carrying 32 people at 22 miles per hour (35 km/h), powered by a 20-horsepower (15 kW) petrol engine with electric transmission, driving a generator that supplied power to the gyro motors and air compressor. The balancing system used a pneumatic servo, not friction wheels, and the gyros were located in the cab, though Brennan planned to reposition them under the floor before a public display, which was delayed due to Scherl’s demonstration. In December 1909, Brennan demonstrated the railcar to the Royal Society, carrying 40 people at 40 km/h (25 mph) on a 200-meter (660 ft) circular track, with dimensions 12.2 m × 4.0 m × 3.0 m (40 ft × 13 ft × 10 ft). The public debut at the Japan-British Exhibition in London in 1910 carried 50 passengers at 20 miles per hour (32 km/h), with Winston Churchill among the attendees. Interest led to the production of children’s clockwork monorail toys in England and Germany. Despite being a viable transport option, the monorail failed to attract further investment; of the two vehicles built, one was sold as scrap and the other used as a park shelter until 1930. Just as Brennan completed testing, August Scherl announced a public demonstration of his gyro monorail in Berlin on 10 November 1909 at the Berlin Zoological Gardens. Scherl’s full-size vehicle was smaller, measuring 5.5 by 1.2 m (18 by 4 ft), with only four passenger seats. It used vertical-axis gyros, weighing 57 kg (125 lb), rotating at 8,000 revolutions per minute, with a hydraulic servomechanism and electric propulsion. Two safety features were included: the gyros continued rotating for several hours without power, allowing safe stopping before balance loss, and small corner wheels could be lowered to stabilize the vehicle. Scherl provided financial backing, while Paul Fröhlich invented the righting mechanism and Emil Falcke designed the car. A Scientific American editorial questioned practicality due to potential rail and bridge modifications. Though well-received during demonstrations, Scherl failed to secure financial support and wrote off his investment. After Brennan and Scherl’s efforts failed, Pyotr Shilovsky continued development in London, using a different balancing principle that allowed a smaller, slower-spinning gyroscope. In 1922, the Soviet government began construction of a Shilovsky monorail between Leningrad and Tsarskoe Selo, but funds ran out shortly after. In 1929, at age 74, Brennan developed a gyrocar, which was rejected by a consortium of Austin/Morris/Rover. In October 2022, Technische Hochschule OWL, Bielefeld University of Applied Sciences, Fraunhofer-Institut für Optronik, Systemtechnik und Bildauswertung, and Landeseisenbahn Lippe e. V. presented a gyro-stabilized monorail based on Brennan’s system on a section of the Extertal railway in Germany, called Monocab. Monocab enables bi-directional service on a single track with autonomous, narrow cabins. It was funded in September 2020 by the European Regional Development Fund and the state of North Rhine-Westphalia with 3.6 million euros. The vehicle runs on a single conventional rail and would topple without the balancing system. A spinning wheel is mounted in a gimbal frame with its spin axis perpendicular to the precession axis, aligned such that at equilibrium, the spin, precession, and vehicle roll axes are mutually perpendicular. Forcing the gimbal to rotate causes precession, generating gyroscopic torques about the roll axis, which can right the vehicle when tilted. The wheel tends to align its spin axis with the gimbal axis, rotating the vehicle about its roll axis. Ideally, the control mechanism would be passive, but due to the system’s equilibrium requiring restoration of potential energy, an active servo is necessary. If constant side forces were resisted by gyroscopic action alone, the gimbal would rotate to stops, causing the vehicle to topple; instead, the mechanism causes the vehicle to lean into disturbances, resisting them with a component of weight. Inertial side forces from cornering cause the vehicle to lean into the corner, but a single gyro introduces asymmetry, leading to net side forces. To ensure correct banking, the gyroscopic torque from vehicle turn rate must be removed. A free gyro maintains orientation relative to inertial space, and rotating it about an axis perpendicular to its spin axis generates gyroscopic moments. However, when the control system deflects the gyro relative to the chassis—not inertial space—vehicle pitch and yaw introduce additional unwanted torques, causing instability in one direction and increased stability in the opposite. Shilovsky encountered this with his road vehicle, which could not make sharp left turns. Brennan and Scherl solved this with pairs of counter-rotating gyros, precessing in opposite directions, so that vehicle motion relative to inertial space produces equal and opposite torques, canceling out the effects. Shilovsky claimed difficulty with double-gyro systems, though the reason is unclear; his solution was to vary control loop parameters with turn rate to maintain balanced response in both directions. Offset loads and side winds cause the vehicle to lean until the center of gravity is above the support point, resulting in contact side forces that may cause more discomfort than cornering forces. These forces create a gimbal deflection bias, which can be used as input to a slower loop to shift the center of gravity laterally, keeping the vehicle upright. This combination of gyro and lateral center of gravity shift is described in a 1962 patent and was implemented in a vehicle built in the US in 1962 by Ernest F. Swinney, Harry Ferreira, and Louis E. Swinney, known as the Gyro-Dynamics monorail. Shilovsky claimed benefits such as reduced right-of-way issues due to steeper gradients and sharper corners, and a form of on-track braking that could offer much shorter stopping distances than conventional rail braking, reducing safe train separation and increasing track occupancy and capacity. He also claimed his designs were lighter than equivalent duo-rail vehicles, with the gyro mass accounting for 3–5% of the vehicle weight, comparable to the bogie weight saved by single-track design. For a vehicle negotiating a horizontal curve, if the gyro axis is vertical, a component of turn rate (Ω) acts about the gimbal pivot, introducing an additional gyroscopic moment into the roll equation, displacing the roll from the correct bank angle and altering the constant term in the characteristic equation. If the turn rate exceeds a critical value, the balancing loop becomes unstable. However, an identical gyro spinning in the opposite direction cancels the destabilizing roll torque and, when forced to precess in the opposite direction, produces a corrective control torque. In 1972, Canada’s Division of Mechanical Engineering rejected a monorail proposal based on this instability issue, though their analysis was limited to single vertical-axis gyro systems and not universally applicable. Gas turbine engines operate with peripheral speeds up to 400 meters per second (1,300 ft/s), and have done so reliably for decades. An estimate for a 10-tonne (9.8 long tons; 11 short tons) vehicle with a center-of-gravity height of 2 meters (6 ft 7 in), assuming half the peripheral speed of jet engines, results in a gyro mass of only 140 kilograms (310 lb), making Brennan’s recommendation of 3–5% of vehicle mass highly conservative.
